title: Containerizing an AI service with Docker
description: Package application code with clear runtime, storage, and secret boundaries.
objectives: Create a container with a limited build context and non-root process
explanation: A container image packages application files, dependencies, and startup instructions. A running container adds process state and a writable layer. Use a Dockerfile to describe the image, and a .dockerignore file to exclude private datasets, credentials, caches, and irrelevant files from the build context.

Copy dependency manifests before frequently changing source when useful for build caching. Choose and maintain a supported base image, and use a non-root account for the application. Supply secrets at runtime through the deployment platform rather than baking them into image layers.

Decide where models and indexes live. Large weights may be mounted or fetched through a controlled provisioning step; persistent data must not depend on a disposable container layer. Bound memory and startup time, expose a readiness check, and verify a restart can reconnect to required services.

terms.definition: A packaged filesystem and startup configuration for containers.
Files available to the image build process.
Storage attached to a container with a lifecycle independent of its writable layer.

example: The supplied Dockerfile packages a small standard-library health endpoint as a non-root user. Copy Dockerfile and health_service.py into an empty exercise directory, build with docker build -t ai-health-demo ., then run with docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 ai-health-demo. It contains no model server.
mistakes: Copying an entire private working directory into an image.
Embedding API keys using Dockerfile ENV.
Keeping the only copy of an index in a disposable container layer.
exercise: Build the health demo in a separate directory and request /health. Stop and restart the container, inspect its configured user, and explain which additional readiness check an actual model service would need.

questions.question: How does an image differ from a running container?
questions.answer: An image is a package; a container is a running instance with runtime state.
questions.distractor: An image is always a running virtual machine.

questions.question: What should .dockerignore exclude from an AI service build?
questions.answer: Secrets, private data, caches, and other files not required by the image.

questions.question: An index disappears after container replacement. What design issue is likely?
questions.answer: It was stored only in the disposable writable layer instead of appropriate persistent storage.
questions.distractor: All vector indexes are inherently temporary.

questions.question: Why inject secrets at runtime?
questions.answer: It avoids distributing credentials inside image layers and supports controlled rotation.
questions.distractor: It makes secret values safe to print in logs.

questions.question: Does a healthy HTTP process prove the model is ready?
questions.answer: No. Readiness may also need to check model loading and required dependencies.
questions.distractor: Yes, any open port proves inference works.
